opus-5.5.text:
I think we're still at a fairly early stage, maybe comparable to where language models were before the scaling picture became clear. There's a lot of excitement, and the demos are impressive. You see robots folding clothes, making coffee, doing fairly dexterous manipulation. But if you look closely, most of these systems are still quite narrow. They work well in the settings they were trained on and degrade quickly when the environment, the objects, or the task change a bit.

To me, the core bottleneck is data. With language, the internet gave us an enormous, diverse corpus almost for free. Robotics has nothing like that. Teleoperation data is expensive and slow to collect, simulation has a real sim-to-real gap, and human video doesn't tell you the actions or forces involved. So a lot of the current work is really about finding a scalable data recipe: mixing teleop, sim, video, and data from many different robot bodies, and figuring out what actually transfers.

The second point is that the field hasn't fully settled on the right abstraction. Should the model be one big end-to-end vision-language-action policy? Or a language or vision model handling high-level reasoning, plus a separate low-level controller? People are betting on different answers, and I don't think the evidence is decisive yet. My intuition is that the strong prior knowledge in pretrained multimodal models is very valuable for generalization. But the physical, contact-rich part of manipulation needs something that current pretraining doesn't really give you.

Third, evaluation is hard. In language you can run a benchmark overnight. In robotics, every evaluation involves real hardware, resets, and variance, so it's hard to know whether one method is truly better than another. That slows the iteration loop a lot. I think whoever builds a faster, more reliable feedback loop, whether through better simulation, world models, or large real-world fleets, will have a big advantage.

So overall I'm optimistic about the direction, but I'd say we haven't had our "GPT-3 moment" in robotics yet. We have promising signs of generalization, but not a clear scaling law that tells you, if you put in ten times more data and compute, you reliably get a much more general robot. Finding that recipe is the most important open question right now.

r001.rationale: The response says current robot systems are narrow, work well in trained settings, and degrade when environments, objects, or tasks change, indicating optimization for particular scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd describe it as being roughly where language models were right before GPT-2, maybe just before. Which sounds dismissive, but I actually mean it as an optimistic statement, because we know what came after that moment.

Let me explain what I mean. The core breakthrough in language models wasn't really the transformer, it was the discovery that you could get a general-purpose prior for free by pretraining on internet-scale text, and then everything downstream, including RL, became tractable because you weren't starting from zero. In robotics we don't have that yet. The thing that's missing is the prior. Internet video gives you a lot about how the world looks and roughly how things move, but it doesn't give you the action side, the actual low-level control. So people are trying to manufacture that prior through teleoperation data, through simulation, through VLA-style models that bootstrap off vision-language models. All of these are reasonable, but none of them has clearly become the "internet text" of robotics, and until one does, scaling laws in robotics are going to look noisy and disappointing.

The second thing I'd say is that robotics is still mostly in what I'd call the imitation era rather than the RL era. Most of the impressive demos you see are behavior cloning on a lot of demonstrations. That works, but it has the same ceiling that imitation always has: you can't exceed your data, and you can't recover well from states the demonstrator never visited. The interesting transition, the one that happened in language with RLHF and then with reasoning models, is when the model starts learning from its own experience and from verifiable outcomes. For robots that's much harder because the environment is the real world, it's slow, it's expensive, and resetting is painful. So the bottleneck is really about building environments and reward signals, not about model architecture. I keep saying the same thing about language agents, and I think it applies even more strongly here.

The third thing, and this is the part I'm most uncertain about, is what the "unit of generalization" is. In language, once you had a good base model, a single model could handle essentially any task because tasks all live in the same text space. In robotics, embodiment differs, sensors differ, the physics differs. It's not obvious a single model across all robots is the right abstraction, or whether you want a general "brain" with embodiment-specific adapters. My guess is the general direction wins eventually, because it always has, but the timeline is probably longer than the current hype suggests.

So, to summarize: the models are not the bottleneck, the data and the environments are. We're pre-GPT-2 in terms of having a scalable recipe, but post-GPT-2 in terms of knowing roughly what we're looking for. That's a strange and actually quite exciting place to be, because the path is visible even if it's not paved yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics as being in an imitation era and notes differences in embodiment, sensors, and physics. It does not suggest robot models are in a feature-engineering era or that they are optimized for particular environments or scenarios.

astra-6.text:
I think robot models are still at a relatively early stage. We’ve seen encouraging progress, but there’s a big difference between getting a robot to demonstrate a task and getting it to perform reliably in a new environment.

One useful way to think about this is to separate understanding from execution. A model might understand “please clean up the table,” but turning that into physical actions requires much more: recognizing what can be moved, choosing a grasp, responding when something slips, and knowing whether the task is actually finished. A small mistake changes the environment, so the robot has to keep observing and adjusting.

Data is another major challenge. Language models can learn from enormous amounts of text, whereas robot interaction data is much harder to collect. And experience collected with one robot or in one setting may not transfer straightforwardly to another.

So I’m optimistic, but I would judge progress less by how impressive a single demonstration looks and more by how consistently a system succeeds across different conditions—and how well it recovers when things go wrong. That’s the gap between an interesting model and a useful robot.

r001.rationale: The response says robot performance may not transfer across environments and settings, but does not suggest that models are still in a feature-engineering era or that they are optimized for particular environments or scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robot models are still at a relatively early stage. We’re seeing promising results, but there’s a big gap between a robot completing a task in a demonstration and reliably handling the same task in an unfamiliar environment.

One difficulty is data. With language, we have a huge amount of text that already exists. For robots, collecting useful interaction data is much more expensive. And when a robot fails, it isn’t always obvious whether the problem is perception, planning, or low-level control. A stronger model can help, but it doesn’t automatically solve the entire system.

So I’m optimistic about general-purpose robot models, but I’d judge progress by how well they generalize and recover from mistakes. Can the robot deal with an object it hasn’t seen before? Can it recognize that an action failed and try something else? Those capabilities matter a lot more for practical use than a single impressive demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response describes an early stage and a gap in generalizing from demonstrations to unfamiliar environments, but it does not suggest that robot models are in a feature-engineering era or are being optimized for particular environments or scenarios.
